questions.prompt: In which state are the particles FARTHEST apart?
options: They are the same in all states
questions.explain: Gas particles are far apart and spread out to fill their container.

questions.prompt: Sort each description into the state it describes.

items.label: Takes the shape of its container but keeps its volume

questions.hint: Think about how free the particles are to move in each state.
questions.explain: Solid: fixed shape, particles vibrate. Liquid: fixed volume, particles slide past each other. Gas: fills the container, particles move fast everywhere.

questions.prompt: Which are ideas of the particle model? Choose all that apply.
options: All matter is made of tiny particles
There are forces of attraction between particles
The gaps between particles are filled with air
questions.hint: Two of these are common mix-ups from the lesson.
questions.explain: Particles don't change size, and the gaps between them are empty space, not air.

questions.prompt: What do the particles in an ice cube do?

feedback.0: Solid particles are never completely still. They always vibrate.

questions.explain: Particles in a solid vibrate about fixed positions.

questions.text: A liquid has a fixed ___ but no fixed ___. The forces of attraction between particles are strongest in a ___.
questions.explain: Liquids keep their volume but take the shape of the container. Solids have the strongest forces of attraction.

questions.prompt: Match each everyday observation to its particle explanation.

pairs.left: A gas fills a whole room
pairs.right: Particles move freely in all directions

pairs.left: Milk takes the shape of the glass
pairs.right: Particles can slide past each other
Particles are held in fixed positions

pairs.left: You can squash the air in a pump
pairs.right: There are large spaces between particles

questions.explain: Every property of a state can be explained by how the particles are arranged and how they move.

questions.prompt: Oxygen melts at −218 °C and boils at −183 °C. What state is it at room temperature (25 °C)?
questions.hint: Is 25 °C above or below the boiling point?
questions.explain: 25 °C is far above oxygen's boiling point (−183 °C), so oxygen is a gas at room temperature.

questions.prompt: Candle wax melts at about 60 °C. A candle sits in a room at 35 °C. What state is the wax in?
questions.explain: 35 °C is below the melting point of 60 °C, so the wax stays solid.

questions.prompt: Put the states in order: from the STRONGEST forces of attraction between particles to the WEAKEST.
questions.explain: Forces of attraction are strongest in solids, weaker in liquids, and weakest in gases.

questions.prompt: Why does a gas completely fill any container it is put in?
options: Gas particles move fast in all directions and attract each other only weakly
Gas particles are attracted to the container walls
questions.explain: Gas particles have high kinetic energy and very weak attraction, so they spread out until they fill the whole space.

questions.prompt: Use the particle model to explain why coconut oil is solid on a cold morning but liquid in the afternoon.
questions.modelAnswer: In the morning the temperature is below coconut oil's melting point (about 24 °C), so its particles have less energy and stay in fixed positions: it is solid. In the afternoon it is warmer, the particles gain energy and move faster, overcome some of the attraction and slide past each other: it becomes liquid.
rubric: I said particles gain energy / move faster when warmer
I described particles in the solid as fixed and in the liquid as sliding past each other
questions.explain: A good particle explanation always links temperature → energy → particle movement → state.
